html: Engineers use an offline suite such as ABB RobotStudio or FANUC ROBOGUIDE. They import the car body CAD data, generate weld paths, simulate the two robots together to avoid collisions, and estimate cycle time. ROBOGUIDE's virtual controller, for example, calculates and validates cycle times, and its SpotPRO package balances spot-welding tasks across several robots while avoiding collisions.[17] When the line shuts down for changeover, the program is downloaded and the technician spends a few hours touching up calibration frames before production restarts.

Three questions run through the lesson. The first is what can physically hold the part. The second is what the controller needs to know about the tool bolted to it. The third is how the program finds out whether the tool actually did its job. The answers involve mechanics, tool configuration and input/output (I/O) programming in URScript and ABB RAPID.

Pick-and-place is the first program most robot programmers write. It is still one of the most common jobs in a factory: take a part from one place and put it down somewhere else. The earlier lessons in this chapter gave you the pieces. You have seen motion types (MoveJ and MoveL), the RAPID and URScript languages (2.3), and how a gripper is switched by a digital output (2.5). This lesson puts them together into one working cycle in a simulator. It then shows how to keep it working when the fixture moves: teaching targets relative to the fixture instead of relative to the robot.

In industrial automation, discrete input and output signals operate primarily on direct current. Sinking and sourcing terminology applies only to DC input and output circuits.[1] Alternating current (AC) circuits reverse polarity continuously, so sinking and sourcing concepts do not apply to them. Direct current circuits maintain fixed positive and negative polarities. Sinking or sourcing input and output points can conduct current in one direction only.[1] Wiring devices to a PLC or robot controller therefore means knowing which way current enters and leaves each terminal. That is because it flows in one direction through solid-state switches and optical isolators.

Nodes represent objects, variables, and executable methods. References connect nodes into an address space graph. For example, a robot controller's OPC UA server could model an arm as a parent Object node named RobotArm containing child Object nodes for each axis (Joint1 through Joint6). In that model, each joint provides Variable nodes for position and velocity with engineering units, alongside Method nodes to trigger calibration routines.
